segments.text: The crew that fires a modern howitzer
almost never sees what it hits.
A shell leaves the barrel at something
like 800 meters a second,
climbs several commotors into the air,
and takes the better part of a minute
to come down on a target the gunners cannot see,
are not looking at, and may not be able to name.
By the time it lands,
the gun that fired it has already packed up and driven away.
The strangest thing about artillery
is that the weapon and the person it kills
are never in the same picture.
So here is the question.
How does a gun hit something it cannot see
from a distance of 20 or 30 km with a shell
that is only a lump of steel following an arc?
And why do armies keep buying
so many different kinds of guns
when they could just buy the biggest one?
The answer is a set of trades.
Every design gives up one thing to gain another,
and the tubes you see on a battlefield
are what is left after the arguments are over.
Start with the oldest trade,
which is weight against range.
A longer barrel keeps the expanding gas
pushing the shell for longer,
so it leaves faster and goes farther.
A heavier shell carries more explosive.
Both make a gun bigger,
and a bigger gun is harder to move,
harder to hide, and slower to set up.
Take the modern 155 millimeter gun
used by most Western armies.
With ordinary shells,
it reaches around 20 to 30 km.
Put in a longer barrel,
a rocket-assisted shell,
or one with a small gas generator in its base,
and that goes up to roughly 40.
Each extra kilometer costs weight, money, and barrel life.
That last cost is easy to forget.
A barrel is a steel pipe being struck by a controlled explosion again and again,
and the heat and friction wear the rifling smooth.
At full charge, it lasts a few thousand rounds at best.
Worn barrels slow the shell down,
and a shell that leaves slower lands short.
So the crew keeps a log of every round fired,
and the charge used,
and the computer corrects for the gun's own age.
The gun is not a fixed tool.
It is a machine that gets slowly less accurate with every shot.
There is a quiet choice hiding in the word howitzer.
A pure gun fires on a flat arc,
and is good at reaching far in a straight line.
A howitzer is built to fire over a wide range of angles,
with charges that can be added or removed.
So the same barrel can drop a shell behind a ridge with a small charge,
or send it far with a large one.
Modern field artillery is almost entirely howitzers,
because being able to choose the arc matters more than a single perfect one.
Rate of fire runs into the same wall.
A well-drilled crew with a loading system can fire several rounds in the first minute,
but the barrel heats with every shot,
so the pace a gun can keep up for an hour is a small fraction of its opening burst.
An automatic loader helps the crew, not the steel.
A short, violent first minute followed by a slow afternoon
is why artillery is timed so carefully.
Mortars are the opposite answer.
A mortar is a plain tube fired at a steep angle,
and the shell drops almost straight down.
It has a short range but weighs little enough that a few soldiers can carry it,
and that is what gives infantry its own artillery, without waiting for anybody.
The steep arc also reaches targets behind hills and walls,
which a flat firing gun cannot.
A mortar gives up distance to be with the infantry,
and the infantry accepts that gladly.
The next trade is between towing and driving.
A towed howitzer is cheap, light, and easy to hide,
but it takes minutes to unhitch, aim, and fire, and minutes to hitch up and leave.
A self-propelled one puts the gun on tracks or wheels with an armored cab,
so it can stop, fire, and drive on in less than a minute,
though it costs far more and burns fuel.
That speed matters because of what the enemy has.
It has radars that can see a shell in flight, trace its arc back, and compute where the gun is.
Within a minute or two, counter-battery fire can be on its way.
That threat created a whole style, it is called shoot and scoot.
The gun moves into a firing position, fires a few rounds, and leaves before the answer arrives.
The best crews can do this in under a minute.
Hiding is no longer enough because the radar does not need to see the gun, only the shell.
The same radar cannot see a gun that is not firing,
so the gun that wins is the one that fires least from any one place.
A position used twice is a position the enemy has already marked.
All of that assumes the gun has already been told where to aim,
which is where the invisible part of artillery begins.
Somebody, a forward observer, a drone or a radar,
sees the target and sends coordinates to a fire direction center,
where a computer works out the angle, the charge, and the direction.
It has to account for wind, air temperature, the wear on that barrel,
and even the temperature of the propellant in the charge bags.
Then the crew loads, and the observer corrects the next shell by saying where the first one fell.
That loop, observe, calculate, fire, correct, decides how fast artillery works.
One trick shows how much arithmetic is going on.
A single gun can fire several shells at different angles and charges,
so that they all land at the same moment.
A low flat shot takes less time than a high one, so the crew fires the high one first,
and the shells arrive together on a target that had no warning of the first.
Several guns can do it as well.
A gun that fires four shells in under a minute has, with a little timing,
done the work of four guns on the same spot.
Accuracy used to come from volume.
A battery fired a whole belt of shells to be sure that some would land close,
which is why 20th century wars use so much ammunition.
Guided shells change that.
A shell with a GPS receiver in its nose and small fins that steer it
can land within a few meters of the point it was told,
so a single round can do the job that dozens did before.
The price is high, a guided shell costs many times as much as an ordinary one,
and a jammer can blind it.
So armies mostly keep both, cheap shells for volume
and expensive ones for the targets that matter.
The shell itself is also a choice.
A fuse can make it explode on impact, a moment after impact,
or in the air above the target, where fragments rain down on people sheltering in a trench.
Some shells carry smoke, some illumination, some a charge that scatters smaller bomblets.
Each is a different answer to a different target,
and the crew picks the fuse and the charge in the same few seconds it takes to load.
The same barrel can shield and advance with smoke and punish an entrenched position with fragments.
And here the problem is no longer the gun at all, it is the supply.
A heavy artillery campaign can fire thousands of rounds a day,
and everyone is about 40 kilograms of metal, charge and fuse that has to travel by truck from a factory.
Production lines for 155 millimeter shells, which used to run slowly in peacetime,
became a strategic problem when wars in Europe started using them faster than factories could make them.
Moving that many shells needs trucks, depots and people to unload them,
so the problem lands straight back in the logistics chain from earlier in this series.
A gun without ammunition is a very expensive monument.
There is a dry joke in how people talk about this.
Artillery is called the king of battle, and then it spends most of its life hiding and moving,
and its most important member is the one who is most often away from the gun.
The observer with a radio, a drone operator in a trench, a radar crew in a van.
They are the real sharp end.
The gun is the muscle, and everything that tells it where to hit is the brain.
So most of the money spent on modern artillery goes on things that do not shoot.
Which brings us to what is easy to get wrong.
People picture artillery as a fight between guns, the bigger one winning.
In practice, the contest is mostly between sensors and speed.
Who can find the other's gun first and answer inside the time it takes a shell to fly?
That is my own reading, not a rule from a manual,
but it suggests that the decisive thing about a modern howitzer is not its caliber.
It is how quickly it can leave.
So return to the crew that never sees its target.
Every part of the system, the long barrel, the steep arc, the radar,
the observer, and the computer is there to close one gap,
the distance between the gun and the thing it has to hit.
And every part of it works to keep the gun from being found in the minute it takes the shell to arrive.
